research_text:
# Research brief: `SSLContextSpec` / `UnsafeProtocol`

## 1. API and meaning of the finding

`javax.net.ssl.SSLContext` represents a secure-socket protocol implementation and acts as a factory for secure socket factories and `SSLEngine` instances. It is initialized with key managers, trust managers, and a source of randomness. `getInstance(protocol)` requests a context implementation by its **protocol name**; `getProtocol()` returns the name supplied when that context was created. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

The reported message is consistent with a check of a **requested `getInstance` protocol string**: it reports `SSL` rather than an accepted name. It does **not**, by itself, establish the protocols enabled on a socket or engine, the protocol negotiated in a handshake, or a runtime vulnerability. The supplied diagnostic alone does not establish the exact invocation or detector implementation. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

**Source:** https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html

## 2. Documented usage and remediation guidance

Oracle documents both `SSL` and `TLS` as standard context algorithm names. `TLS` supports some version of TLS and may support other SSL/TLS versions. Even the version-specific names `TLSv1.2` and `TLSv1.3` **may support other versions**; the context name alone is not an enabled-protocol restriction. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))

For a context requiring initialization, Oracle documents `init` with key managers, trust managers and randomness. Null arguments are API-valid and request the applicable provider/default implementations. Oracle also documents an immediately usable default context through `getDefault()`. These API semantics differ from the CrySL rule’s requirements. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

Oracle’s documentation describes controls for enabled protocols, including socket/engine settings and `SSLParameters.setProtocols`. Its JSSE guide also documents runtime restrictions such as `jdk.tls.disabledAlgorithms`. These controls are distinct from the context-name predicate. Oracle recommends `X509ExtendedTrustManager` over the legacy interface for JSSE provider and trust-manager implementations; endpoint identification is separately configured through `SSLParameters`. ([oracle.com](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/8u261-relnotes.html?utm_source=openai))

The cited API documentation does **not** prescribe a universal replacement for every use of `SSL`, nor does it say that changing only the context name guarantees a particular negotiated version. A provider-selected `TLS` context is documented; its effective protocols remain provider- and configuration-dependent. Do not weaken certificate validation or hostname verification when changing configuration. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))

**Sources:**

- https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html#sslcontext-algorithms
- https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html
- https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/oracle-providers.html

## 3. Compatibility and migration

- **Platform support:** Java SE 25 requires implementations to support `TLSv1.2` and `TLSv1.3`; that is not a guarantee for older Java releases or every provider. Oracle JDK 11 included TLS 1.3, and Oracle JDK 8u261 added it to JDK 8. The 8u261 release notes say TLS 1.3 was disabled for the default `SSL`/`TLS` context at the client endpoint in that release and document ways to enable it. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))
- **Wire compatibility:** Oracle notes that TLS 1.3 is not directly compatible with earlier versions. Its documented migration risks include different close behavior, cipher suites and session-resumption behavior, and lack of DSA signature support in TLS 1.3. The 8u261 notes document protocol-configuration mechanisms and a close-notify compatibility property; these are version-specific guidance, not a universal migration path. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html?utm_source=openai))
- **Persisted formats:** The consulted `SSLContext` and JSSE documentation does not document a keystore or other persisted-format conversion required merely to change the requested context name. It does not establish compatibility for an application’s particular stored data, certificates, provider, or configuration.

**Sources:**

- https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/8u261-relnotes.html
- https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html

## 4. Exact supplied CrySL rule

The supplied source declares `SPEC javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`. Its `Get` matching clause is: ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

```text
	g1: getInstance(protocol);
	g2: getInstance(protocol, _);
	Get := g1 | g2;
```

The source declares `protocol` as `java.lang.String` and gives this condition: ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

```text
	protocol in {"TLSv1.2", "TLSv1.3"};
```

Thus, the source specifies `getInstance` events with **one or two arguments**: the first is the declared `protocol` variable, and the second is `_` in the two-argument form. The rule is scoped to `javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`; it is **not a name-only rule for an unrelated class’s method**. The source itself does not describe the detector’s method-resolution implementation. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

The same source declares `init(km, tm, random)` and zero- and two-argument `createSSLEngine` events, orders them as `Get, Init, Engine?`, and forbids `getDefault()`. It also declares the three initialization-argument predicates. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

**Important discrepancy:** the reported message lists `TLS` as accepted, but this CrySL source’s literal constraint lists only `TLSv1.2` and `TLSv1.3`. The source does not explain the message’s presentation or establish which compiled rule produced it. The linked `master` source is mutable; the supplied SHA-256 was not independently verified in this research pass.

**Rule source:** https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl
